title-group.article-title: Raw Ocimum sanctum L. leaf extract modulates the pharmacokinetic of ceftriaxone and increases its bioavailability in staphylococcal mastitis

sec.title: BACKGROUND:
sec.p: To study the pharmacokinetic interaction of cephalosporin antibiotic ceftriaxone (CFT) with raw undiluted Ocimum sanctum L. leaf juice in chronic staphylococcal mastitis in caprine.

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS:
sec.p: Chronic inflammation of the udder was evoked in goats by Staphylococcus aureus (J638) intracisternal inoculation 2000 cfu for 30 days into the left udder. Animals of Group I were given one single dose of CFT at 20 mg/kg i.v. Group II animals were given one single dose of CFT at 20 mg/kg i.v, and contemporary extracted fresh leaf juice of O. sanctum L. given at 5 ml/kg orally for 7 consecutive days.

sec.title: RESULTS:
sec.p: O. sanctum L. at 5 ml/kg oral had synergistic herb–drug pharmacokinetic interaction with CFT antibiotic (i.v.) and increased its bioavailability. It prolonged its rate of elimination (β) and enhanced the volume of distribution (Vdarea) and mean residence time in the body. Bioavailability and persistence of the antibiotic CFT and its metabolite ceftizoxime were increased in the milk from the udder.

sec.title: CONCLUSION:
sec.p: Administration of O. sanctum L. at 5 ml/kg oral with intravenous CFT at 20 mg/kg may be advocated for effective treatment of S. aureus inflammation of the udder in caprine.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The causes of inflammation of the udder are many, and the impact on public health and the economy is enormous. In India, the incidence rate of mastitis in caprine ranges from 2.18% to 13.13%.[1] Among it’s causes, Staphylococcus aureus is the most prevalent worldwide.[2] It is of public health importance because the enterotoxins made by S. aureus cause gastrointestinal disorders and food poisoning.[3] Effective treatment of inflamed udder continues to be a matter of analysis. Among the various ways followed for the treatment of mastitis, antibiotic medical aid could be a common application. The effectiveness of antibiotics is often optimized by maintaining the concentration of the drug higher than the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) at the site of infection for a longer period.[4]

Many reports signify the role of herbs and herbal extracts/preparations have bio-enhancing action and higher bactericide action. One among them is black tulsi (O. sanctum L.). Earlier reports stated that the O. sanctum aqueous extract (at 60 mg/kg) had a greater inhibition zone against Proteus sp., Escherichia coli, S. aureus, Klebsiella sp., etc., compared to its alcoholic extract.[5] As suggested in some studies, O. sanctum leaf extract (aqueous) significantly reduced lactoperoxidase activity and accelerated speedy recovery to normalcy in chromosomal injury and radiation morbidity due to lipid peroxidation in the liver by radiation.[6]

Herbal medicines are a bit complicated mixture of different bioactive ingredients, which can act with medication through pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic mechanisms and generally end in grievous consequences.[7] As reported, pharmacokinetics and/or pharmacodynamic effects may occur due to herb–drug interaction,[8] that supposed to increase concern over the security of the use of herbal products with medication.[9] Thus, it is vital to understand the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions caused by the coadministration of herbal products and medicines to avoid undesirable effects if any. It is going to have synergistic or antagonistic action producing useful or adverse impact. Hence, within the given study, we tend to study the pharmacokinetic interaction of O. sanctum L. leaf juice on single dose ceftriaxone (CFT) antibiotic injection i.v. in induced chronic inflammation of udder in goat.

sec.title: Induction of chronic mastitis
sec.p: 2000 cfu of S. aureus (J638) coagulase +ve strains were inoculated into the left teat canal in 12 healthy lactating black Bengal goats to induce chronic inflammation of the udder.[1011] The protocol was approved by IAEC (EC/94/dt.24/06/2011).

sec.title: Identification of plant
sec.p: For identification, voucher specimen of O. Sanctum L. was deposited (no. WBUAFS01) to the Botanical Survey of India.

sec.title: Antibiotic sensitivity test
sec.p: The sensitivity of the coagulase +ve S. aureus (J638) to the antibiotic CFT, ceftizoxime (CTZ), and leaf juice of O. sanctum L. was tested in vitro as per CLSI, 2008.[12]

sec.title: Optimum dose selection of Ocimum sanctum L. leaf juice
sec.p: The dose of O. sanctum L. at 5 ml/kg/day oral was decided as per Dash et al. 2016.[13] Briefly, raw tulsi leaf juice was given orally at 5 ml (5.12 g aprox)/kg body weight for 14 days to 6 healthy goats. No abnormalities in terms of feeding, defecation, and urination were observed. Blood samples of day 0, 3rd, 7th, and 14th day were tested for aspartate transaminase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine (CRT) level. There was no significant change in the AST and ALT activity and CRT and BUN level. Any substances not producing any adverse symptoms at 5000 mg/kg are considered practically nontoxic (OECD 420).

sec.title: Extraction of antibiotic residue in plasma and milk
sec.p: Extraction of antibiotics (CFT and CTZ) in plasma and milk samples was done as per the modified method of Sar et al.[14] To the plasma/urine sample (0.5 mL), the mobile phase (0.5 mL) was added. To this, 2 mL mixture of 70% methanol + 30% sodium acetate (0.1 M) was added making the final volume to 3 mL. pH was adjusted to 5.2 by adding 1–2 drops of high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) grade acetic acid. The final mixture was shaked thoroughly by vertexing for 30 min, and the vertex mixture was kept at 4°C for 15 min. This aliquot was centrifuged at 3000 rpm/15 min. The supernatant was taken and passed through 20 μ syringe filter. 20 μL of the clear supernatant was injected into HPLC with photo diode array detector (Make-SHIMADZU LC-20AT). The chromatographic conditions were set at λ = 254 nm at 1.5 ml/min flow rate in a 5 μ Luna C18 (2); 250 mm × 4.6 mm (RP) column. Limit of detection was 0.01 μg/ml for both CFT and CTZ both in plasma and milk. The mobile phase was prepared as per US pharmacopoeia for the drug CFT. The concentration of the drug recovered in plasma or milk was calculated using the formula,

A2 is sample area
V2 is final sample volume after processing (ml)
V1 is volume of sample taken for processing (ml)
C is concentration of the standard used.

sec.title: In vivo pharmacokinetic analysis
sec.p: On confirmation of chronic mastitis, Group I animals (n = 6) were kept as control and Group II animals (n = 6) were administered with leaf juice of O. santum L. orally at 5 ml/kg. One hour following administration of the undiluted leaf juice, one single dose of CFT at 20 mg/kg i.v. was given. Leaf juice was given once daily at 24 h intervals for 7 days. Blood sample (approx. 2 ml) was collected in heparinized tubes from the jugular vein at 0, 0.08, 24, 48, 72, 96, 96.08, 120, and 144 h postdosing; plasma was separated and preserved at 4°C. Drug concentrations were estimated in HPLC (SHIMADZU LC-20AT, Japan) under the chromatographic conditions as stated earlier.

sec.title: Analysis of residue of antibiotics in milk
sec.p: Two milliliter of milk sample was collected at 0 (predosing), 0.08, 24, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, 168, and 192 h postdosing from both halves of the udder. Drug concentration in milk was estimated in HPLC (SHIMADZU LC-20AT, Japan) under the chromatographic conditions as stated earlier.

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Results were presented as mean ± standard error of the mean, and analysis was done by Student’s t-test using SPSS 10.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, I11., USA).

sec.title: Antibiotic sensitivity test
sec.p: S. aureus (J638) isolate was found sensitive to CFT, CTZ, and undiluted juice of O. sanctum L. leaves.

sec.title: Extraction of antibiotics in plasma and milk
sec.p: In plasma, the recovery was 81.14% ± 0.93% (for CFT) and 80.37% ± 1.03% (for CTZ), respectively, and in milk, the recovery was 79.83% ± 1.28% (for CFT) and 75.56% ± 0.94% (for CTZ), respectively. Figures 1 and 2 represent the chromatograms of CFT and CTZ extracted from plasma and milk, respectively.

sec.title: In vivo pharmacokinetic interaction
sec.p: Figure 3 depicted that the antibiotic CFT was recovered from plasma till 24 h postdosing, whereas its active metabolite CTZ was recovered till 48 h of postdosing of CFT antibiotic in mastitis animals of Group I (n = 6). Both CFT and its metabolite CTZ were available in blood plasma for an extended duration in Group II (n = 6) mastitis animals who were administered with O. Sanctum L. leaf juice [Figure 3]. In Group II animals, CFT could be obtained in plasma up to 48 h postadministration, and its active metabolite CTZ was detected from 0.5–72 h postdosing of CFT antibiotic.

caption.p: (a) Semi-log plot of mean plasma concentration (μg/ml) of ceftriaxone against time (h) in induced mastitis goats following single-dose intravenous administration of ceftriaxone at 20 mg/kg with (Group II, n = 6) and without (Group I, n = 6) 1 h presingle dose oral administration of Ocimum sanctum L. leaf juice at 5 ml/kg once daily for consecutive 7 days, (b) Semi-log plot of mean plasma concentration (μg/ml) of ceftizoxime against time (h) in induced mastitis goats following single-dose intravenous administration of ceftriaxone at 20 mg/kg with (Group II, n = 6) and without (Group I, n = 6) 1 h presingle dose oral administration of O. sanctum L. leaf juice at 5 ml/kg once daily for consecutive 7 days

sec.p: The differences in the pharmacokinetic parameters of CFT in both groups were given in Table 1. Maximal plasma concentration (C°P) of CFT (C°P) was not significantly different between Group I (C°P = 87.70 ± 5.72 μg/ml) and Group II (C°P = 93.62 ± 5.33 μg/ml) following intravenous injection of CFT at 20 mg/kg. The absorption rate constant and absorption half-life did not differ significantly between Group I (α = 1.79 ± 0.40 h−1; t1/2α = 0.50 h ± 0.10 h) and Group II (α = 1.68 ± 0.24 h−1; t1/2α = 0.47 ± 0.08 h). However, the elimination rate constant (β) and elimination half-life (t1/2 β) were significantly different (P < 0.05) between Group I (β = 0.18 ± 0.03 per h; t1/2 β = 4.92 ± 1.10 h) and Group II (β = 0.09 ± 0.009 h−1; t1/2 β = 7.75 ± 0.72 h). In Group II animals, the volume of distribution of the drug CFT (Vdarea = 0.17 ± 0.01 L/kg) was higher (P < 0.05) in comparison to Group I (Vdarea = 0.09 ± 0.008 L/kg). Significantly higher (P < 0.05) mean residence time (MRT) was seen in Group II (MRT = 5.73 ± 0.48 h) than in Group I (MRT = 4.26 ± 0.75 h).

caption.p: Kinetic parameters of ceftriaxone following single dose intravenous administration at 20 mg kg−1 without (Group I, n=6) and with (Group II, n=6) oral administration of Ocimum sanctum L. leaf juice at 5 mL kg−1 once daily for consecutive 7 days in induced mastitis in goat

sec.title: Residue of antibiotics in milk
sec.p: There was scanty milk secretion from the left udder in Group I animals due to inoculation of bacterial colony though the left teat canal for induction of mastitis. In Group I animals, due to scanty milk secretion from the left udder, the antibiotic concentration could not be determined in the milk sample from the left udder. In the right udder, CFT was not obtained, but CTZ which is its active metabolite was obtained in milk samples collected at 8, 12, and 24 h postdosing of CFT (i.v.) [Figure 4]. In contrast, in Group II animals, CFT was detected in milk samples collected at 96–120 h postdosing in both halves of the udder. CTZ was obtained in milk samples of 96–144 h postdosing in the left udder and from 0.5 to 144 h postdosing in the right [Figure 5] udder.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Among various causes, S. aureus is the most prevalent cause of mastitis throughout the world. CFT is frequently prescribed by veterinarians in clinical mastitis cases in goats when it is sensitive to the microorganisms. As reported by Dash et al. in 2016,[13] O. sanctum L. leaf juice (0.05ml) decreased the MIC of CFT and CTZ antibiotic against S. aureus (J638) to 0.5 μg/ml which were 3 μg/ml and 1 μg/ml, respectively, when leaf juice of O. sanctum L. was not given. As reported earlier by Dash et al. 2014,[11] S. aureus (J638) strain is sensitive to antibiotic ceftriaxone (CFT). Hence, during this study, CFT was used as the antibiotic at 20 mg/kg i.v. in S. aureus (J638)-induced inflammation of the udder in goat and it's pharmacokinetic modulation was studied by oral administration of raw leaf juice of O. sanctum L. in case of induced chronic mastitis in goat as the tulsi leaf juice had antioxidant and bio-enhancing action in our previous study.[13] The investigated pharmacokinetic interactions of extracted undiluted O. sanctum L. leaf juice with antibiotic CFT against induced chronic inflammation of the udder revealed some significant results.

During this study, it was observed that the pharmacokinetic of the drug CFT was affected by the administration of raw juice of O. sanctum L. leaves. The mean maximal plasma concentration (C0P) of CFT was not affected significantly by ingestion of O. sanctum L. leaf juice with CFT at 20 mg/kg (i.v.) [Figure 3] but prolonged the persistence of the drug and increased the elimination half-life significantly (P < 0.05) in Group II animals (t1/2 β = 7.75 ± 0.72 h) than in Group I animals (t1/2 β = 7.75 ± 0.72 h). This was evident from the lower elimination coefficient (β) of CFT in Group II animals (β = 0.09 ± 0.009 h−1) compared to Group I animals (β = 0.18 ± 0.03 h−1). An increased elimination half-life (t1/2 β) in the semilogarithmic plot indicated toward slower elimination of the antibiotic CFT and prolonged availability of the drug in the body due to ingestion of leaf juice of O. sanctum L. CFT was obtained in plasma in Group I up to 24 h postdosing, whereas in Group II where the animals were administered with the leaf juice, it was obtained in plasma up to 48 h postadministration [Figure 3]. CTZ (the metabolite of CFT) was detected in plasma for a longer duration in Group II animals than in Group I animals. It was available in plasma from 1 to 48 h postdosing in Group I and from 0.5 to 72 h postdosing in Group II [Figure 3]. Thus O. sanctum L. leaf juice may increase the bioavailability of CFT antibiotic in chronic mastitis. This signifies the slow metabolism of the drug CFT which was evident from the lower plasma concentration of the metabolite CTZ detected in the plasma of Group II animals administered with leaf juice than in Group I animals [Figure 3]. This may be due to the inhibition of mixed-function oxidase enzymes because CFT undergoes hydrolysis through mixed function oxidase system to produce CTZ.[15] This was in support of the findings of Samal et al., 2017[1617] which reported that the active ingredients of black tulsi, i.e., eugenol, carvacrol, elemene, caryophyllene, and linalool may inhibit the CYP450 enzyme systems. However, the particular phytochemicals in the raw leaf juice of O. sanctum L. responsible for the observed effect could not be determined here.

Studies on the pharmacokinetics of the antibiotic CFT in different species reported by different groups are noteworthy. One of such study states that following i.v. and i.m. injection of CFT in goat, it gets eliminated in urine in high concentration for 24 h post-dosing.[17] In the milk from lactating goats, its detection was very low. For a therapeutic serum level, a dose of i.m. injection at 20 mg/kg every 12 h was recommended.[17] In ewes, CFT has a poor penetration and distribution from the bloodstream into the mammary gland following i.m injection.[18] The bioavailability was 83.6% and protein binding was 33%. The concentration of the antibiotic was consistently lower in milk than in serum. The area under curve (AUC) (milk)/AUC (serum) and C (max milk)/C (max serum) ratios was <0.4.[18] CFT was injected i.v. route to clinically healthy Akkaraman sheep at 20, 40, and 80 mg/kg. The antibiotic was very well tolerated at these dose levels. The elimination half-life was significantly longer at 40 and 80 mg/kg doses than that of 20 mg/kg dose. In comparison to 20 mg/kg, dose-normalized AUC0–∞ at the 80 mg/kg dose significantly increased (P < 0.05).[19] Following a single dose i.v. injection of CFT at 20 mg/kg in healthy and mastitic crossbred cows, peak mean plasma concentration reached 131.67 ± 1.83 μg/mL at 5 min, that sharply fell until 1 h (35.56 ± 0.44 μg/mL) and was found below the detection limit at 24 h post-dosing in mastitic crossbred cows. In contrast, the active metabolite of CFT (CTZ) attended a peak concentration of 55.42 ± 3.34 μg/mL at 72 h postdosing and could not be obtained at 120 h postdosing in the milk of those mastitic crossbred cows.[20]

It was seen that administration of O. sanctum L. leaf juice in Group II animals significantly increased (P < 0.05) the volume of distribution (Vdarea) of the drug (Vdarea = 0.17 ± 0.01 L/kg) than in Group I (Vdarea = 0.09 ± 0.008 L/kg) [Table 1]. Significantly higher (P < 0.05) MRT was seen in Group II (MRT = 5.73 ± 0.48 h) than in Group I (MRT = 4.26 ± 0.75 h) [Table 1]. Higher Vdarea means more distribution of the drug to other tissues in the extravascular components of the body. A higher MRT of the drug means the average time of stay of the drug in the body of the animal is more.[21] This suggested that the leaf juice of O. sanctum L. enhanced the distribution of the antibiotic CFT to other tissues in the body and increased the average residence time of the antibiotic in the body which is very important for the successful therapy of mastitis which is an infectious inflammatory condition of the udder.

Postdosing milk residue analysis of the antibiotic CFT and its metabolite CTZ revealed that no residue of CFT [Figure 4] could be detected in milk samples from the Group I animals treated with CFT (i.v.) only, but its metabolite CTZ [Figure 5] was detected. This is in congruence to Sar et al. 2018.[22] In Group II animals who were administered with undiluted leaf juice, both CFT and CTZ were detected in both halves of the udder. This suggested that raw leaf juice of O. sanctum L. might have enhanced penetrance of both CFT and CTZ molecules into blood–milk barrier.[2223] Further, the decreased MIC of the antibiotic CFT and CTZ in the presence of undiluted leaf juice of O. sanctum L.(0.05 ml) signified its synergistic bio-enhancing effect.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Leaf juice of O. sanctum L. at 5 ml/kg oral had synergistic herb–drug pharmacokinetic interaction with CFT antibiotic (i.v.) and augmented its bioavailability in S. aureus (J638)-induced chronic mastitis in goat. It slowed down the rate of elimination (β) and increased the volume of distribution (Vdarea) and MRT of the antibiotic CFT in the body. It probably increased the bioavailability and persistence of CFT and its metabolite CTZ in milk by enhancing the penetrance of the drug molecules into the blood–milk barrier. The decreased MIC of the antibiotics CFT and CTZ against S. aureus (J638) in the presence of the undiluted leaf juice signified its synergistic effect. Oral supplementation of undiluted leaf juice of O. sanctum L. at 5 ml/kg with CFT antibiotic at 20 mg/kg (i.v.) may be an effective regimen for the treatment of Staph. aureus chronic inflammation of udder in caprine.
